data.title: Nutex outlines 3 to 5 hospitals per year growth, with 2 openings targeted in Q4 2026
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Nutex Health (NUTX) Q3 2026

Management view

  • “It was another strong quarter with solid financial results, steady collections, important reimbursement developments and continued growth in hospital volumes,” said (Chairman of the Board & CEO Thomas Vo), while pointing to nine-month volume growth and cash generation alongside year-over-year declines in reported revenue and adjusted EBITDA.
  • (CEO Vo) tied the year-over-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA declines primarily to prior-period revenue recognition effects, saying the declines “are not necessarily due to weaker collections in 2026,” and citing “uneven revenue recognition for the first 9 months in 2025” from updated collection estimates and the removal of “ineligible charts.”
  • (CEO Vo) highlighted reimbursement/legal developments under the No Surprises Act and IDR, including that “the District Court in Virginia reached a similar conclusion… bringing the number of states with provider favorable ruling on key IDR issues to at least 7,” and said Nutex “strongly support[s] the Murphy bill” while “firmly oppos[ing] the Pallone proposal.”
  • “For the remainder of 2026, our active development pipeline includes projects in San Antonio, Texas and Jacksonville, Florida, both of which are expected to open in the fourth quarter,” said (CEO Vo), adding that Nutex has “4 additional projects under active construction with expected completion in late 2027 and early 2028.”
  • “Total revenue for Q3 of '26 was $217.6 million compared to $267.8 million for the same period in '25,” said (Chief Financial Officer Jon Bates), attributing the decline largely to 2025’s revenue-per-visit uplift during early IDR realization.

Outlook

  • (CEO Vo) reiterated near-term facility timing, saying, “we have two opening this year, hopefully, before the end of the year, and that's San Antonio and Jacksonville,” and described four additional projects “hoping to open by the end of 2027 and a worst-case scenario beginning of 2028, depending on construction time.”
  • On cost cadence rather than formal guidance, (CFO Bates) said contract services should be “somewhere in that same type of range in relation to revenue, assuming everything else stays the same,” emphasizing the post-HaloMD renegotiation and CMS fee changes.
  • (President & Director Warren Hosseinion) set an expansion target for the Population Health platform, stating, “our goal is to build one to two new IPAs around our hospitals every year.”

Financial results

  • (CEO Vo) reported that for the first three quarters of 2026, “total revenue reached $644.9 million,” “adjusted EBITDA decreased 13%… to $211.4 million,” and “net income attributable to Nutex increased to $152.9 million.”
  • (CFO Bates) detailed Q3 profitability and margin, reporting “operating income… was $77.1 million,” “net income attributable to Nutex was $40.2 million,” and “adjusted EBITDA attributable to Nutex… $63.9 million.”
  • (CFO Bates) described volume and unit economics dynamics, including that hospital division visits rose to “54,622 visits in Q3 of '26,” and discussed IDR pipeline metrics: “approximately 50% to 60% are submitted through the IDR process,” “40% to 50%… resulting in an award determination,” and Nutex “has prevailed in over 80% of those terminations over the last nine months.”
  • (CFO Bates) emphasized liquidity and cash generation, reporting “cash… just under $250 million,” “accounts receivable… $356.1 million,” and “net cash from operating activities… $188.1 million” for the first nine months.

Q&A

  • Jeffrey Cohen, Ladenburg Thalmann: asked to confirm facility openings cadence; (CEO Vo) answered, “we have two opening this year… San Antonio and Jacksonville,” and “four that are under construction… hoping to open by the end of 2027… beginning of 2028.”
  • Jeffrey Cohen, Ladenburg Thalmann: asked about contract services directionally; (CFO Bates) said Nutex has not given “specific guidance,” but expects contract services to remain “somewhere in that same type of range in relation to revenue.”
  • Jeffrey Cohen, Ladenburg Thalmann: asked about noncontrolling interest; (CFO Bates) framed expectations as “somewhere in that high teens to maybe low 20% in relation to gross profit.”
  • Bill Sutherland, StoneX: asked whether revenue per visit under $4,000 is an appropriate range and about capital deployment; (CFO Bates) said “that range is certainly fair,” and on cash said the priority is “opening up facilities and hospitals,” while (CEO Vo) added “External growth, we're still targeting three to five hospitals per year.”
  • Yuan Zhi, B. Riley: asked if payers changed behavior post Fifth Circuit; (CEO Vo) said “payers are still paying,” while (CFO Bates) pointed to “a good solid nine months of cash collections.” Yuan Zhi also asked about policy risk; (CEO Vo) said, “we don't know,” emphasizing the legislative process.
  • Thomas McGovern, Maxim: asked whether lower CMS IDR fee increased provider engagement; (CFO Bates) said it “has slightly increased” but needs “a couple more quarters,” and (CEO Vo) added that the process still takes “four to six months” and “only 5% of providers like us actually do arbitration.” McGovern also asked about Nutex’s award-determination rate; (CFO Bates) said it “has been very consistent” and was added “just for some clarity.”
  • Benjamin Haynor, Lake Street: asked about IPA strategy; (CEO Vo) said, “having an IPA… surrounding your hospital is a great business development strategy,” and (President Hosseinion) added, “we're not trying to be the largest IPA… We're trying to essentially have primary care physician and specialist partners that are near our facilities.” Haynor also asked about physician vs. hospital collections; (CFO Bates) said “nothing material, but something that we're seeing.”
  • Eugene Mannheimer, Prime Executions: asked how many mature hospitals are profitable; (CEO Vo) answered, “the ones that are mature, yeah, I think all of them are profitable,” adding that “Two of those three are profitable already” for the three opened last year. Mannheimer also asked why fewer claims go to IDR; (CFO Bates) said payers are “paying slightly better on the front end.”

Sentiment analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly positive, with repeated focus on reimbursement sustainability, payer behavior, IDR mechanics, and capital allocation; questions pressed on “behavior change from payers,” revenue-per-visit range, and whether Nutex can provide “some guidance around 2027.”
  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and more cautious/neutral in policy discussions, including (CEO Vo) saying “we don't know” on near-term policy change; management repeatedly emphasized monitoring trends “very, very closely” and highlighted cash and expansion priorities.
  • Compared with the prior quarter, management sounded more defensive/cautious around reimbursement/policy uncertainty (legislative proposals) while maintaining confidence on development timing and operational volume growth.

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • The current call added a sharper legislative contrast, with (CEO Vo) stating Nutex “strongly support[s] the Murphy bill” and “firmly oppose[s] the Pallone proposal,” a more explicit policy framing than the prior quarter’s focus on final rules and court wins.
  • Openings expectations narrowed from Q2’s “West Little Rock, Arkansas; San Antonio, Texas; and Jacksonville, Florida… expected to open in the third and fourth quarter of 2026” to Q3’s emphasis on San Antonio and Jacksonville in Q4; West Little Rock was not discussed in the current call.
  • Q3 discussion placed more investor attention on revenue-per-visit normalization and the hospital vs. physician collections gap, which (CEO Vo) described as “slight differences,” while Q2 emphasized cost reductions tied to CMS fees and the HaloMD amendment.

Risks and concerns

  • (CEO Vo) flagged potential adverse legislative outcomes, saying the Pallone proposal “would eliminate the IDR process beginning in 2028,” and management described ongoing insurer practices and compliance issues as a key friction point.
  • (CEO Vo) noted “Physician fee collections are slightly down compared to hospital collection,” and said, “We are continuing to follow this trend closely.”
  • (CFO Bates) cited IDR process frictions that can prevent determinations, including payers providing “not accurate and complete data” and eligibility issues that cause claims to be “kicked back.”

Final takeaway

Management emphasized that Q3 reflected strong visit growth and cash generation alongside revenue and adjusted EBITDA comparisons affected by 2025 revenue-recognition dynamics, while reiterating two hospital openings targeted for Q4 2026 and a multi-project construction pipeline into 2027-2028. Leadership underscored continued reliance on the No Surprises Act/IDR framework for “fair market-based reimbursement,” framed material legislative divergence between the Murphy and Pallone proposals, and described capital deployment priorities centered on new facility development, infrastructure investment, and continued monitoring of physician-collection softness versus hospital collections.

data.title: Koppers forecasts 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $220M-$225M as pricing resets take effect in January 2027
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Koppers Holdings Inc. (KOP) Q3 2026

Management view

  • Chairman & CEO Leroy M. Ball said Q3 showed “underlying momentum in our portfolio” but also “near-term pressure created by continually rising input costs,” adding that “costs for coal tar, copper, diesel, freight, and other raw materials continue to rise and move through our businesses faster than we could recover them through pricing.”

  • Chairman & CEO Leroy Ball attributed resilience to Performance Chemicals and utility poles, saying “Performance Chemicals again delivered strong volume growth…driven by continued momentum in industrial applications and market share gains in our residential business,” while “utility and industrial products continue to benefit from a healthy infrastructure market for utility poles.”

  • Chairman & CEO Leroy Ball linked the earnings outlook revision to cost timing, stating, “That reduced our margins and led us to revise our earnings outlook for the remainder of 2026,” and added, “significant pricing actions will take effect in January 2027 and enable us to recover much of what we have absorbed this year.”

  • CFO & Treasurer Eric Brenner framed the quarter as margin pressure plus cash strength: “Sales increased despite a mixed demand environment…Second, higher raw material and logistics costs, along with lower crosstie pricing, pressured margins…Third, and importantly, we generated record year-to-date operating cash flow and record year-to-date free cash flow.”

Outlook

  • Management reduced full-year profitability targets, with Chairman & CEO Leroy Ball saying, “We revised our forecast lower to reflect higher input costs,” and guiding to 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $220 million to $225 million and 2026 adjusted EPS of $3.10 to $3.25 per share.

  • Chairman & CEO Leroy Ball guided to 2026 free cash flow of $115 million to $135 million, adding that it “has improved due to a $5 million reduction in expected capital expenditures for this year,” alongside total 2026 capital expenditures of “approximately $50 million.”

  • On timing of recovery, Chairman & CEO Leroy Ball said cost pressure would persist near-term: “The dynamic will continue to affect our results through the balance of the year,” while the reset was positioned for 2027: “about 80% of our current book of business is already agreed to for next year at prices that address the increases we are seeing across the board.”

Financial results

  • The company reported Q3 sales of $499 million and adjusted EBITDA of $58 million, with Chairman & CEO Leroy Ball saying results reflected “continually rising input costs,” and CFO & Treasurer Eric Brenner quantifying, “we estimate the year-over-year impact of higher input costs to be $16 million in the third quarter.”

  • CFO & Treasurer Eric Brenner reported profitability compression, stating adjusted EBITDA margin was “11.6% compared to 14.6% in the prior year quarter,” and that adjusted EPS was $0.77 compared with $1.21 in the prior-year quarter.

  • CFO & Treasurer Eric Brenner said cash generation remained a central highlight despite quarterly timing effects, reporting year-to-date operating cash flow of $127 million and year-to-date free cash flow of $92 million, while noting Q3 free cash flow of $19 million “due to timing of working capital items.”

  • CFO & Treasurer Eric Brenner updated leverage and liquidity, stating that as of September 30 the company had $360 million in available liquidity and $845 million of net debt, “representing a net leverage ratio of 3.7x,” and reiterated the “long-term goal of reducing net leverage to 2 to 3x.”

Q&A

  • Gary Prestopino, Barrington Research: Asked which segments would receive price increases and whether it was “across the board”; Chairman & CEO Ball said Performance Chemicals pricing was most advanced, noting “over 80% of our booked business, we have come to agreement with those customers…that will go into effect Jan 1,” while adding RPS would have smaller escalators and that CM&C was “a little bit uncertain.”

  • Gary Prestopino, Barrington Research: Asked whether the Florence plant was “idled or permanently closed”; Chairman & CEO Ball answered, “We are in the process of idling it…we have, at this point in time, not made a decision to permanently close it.”

  • Liam Burke, B. Riley: Pressed on Performance Chemicals share recovery and whether customers were returning; Chairman & CEO Ball said, “we did have a significant share loss…Heading into ’26, we were able to recover some of that,” and added “we have systematically grown our industrial market share over the past 3 to 4 years.”

  • Liam Burke, B. Riley: Asked if industrial was “moving the needle”; Chairman & CEO Ball said, “It’s not a needle mover…The industrial is helpful…but…we need a strong residential market.”

  • Liam Burke, B. Riley: Asked if RUPS margin decline reflected costs and Class I price concessions; Chairman & CEO Ball said it did, and CFO & Treasurer Brenner added it was “the deliberate price concessions that we made to secure volume…as we look to idle Florence.”

  • Michael Mathison, Sidoti: Asked whether lower capex was sustainable; Chairman & CEO Ball said, “my expectation is that $50 million would be the high watermark,” with “$40 million to $45 million” as ongoing needs “under our current portfolio.”

  • Michael Mathison, Sidoti: Asked if the buyback vs. debt paydown mix reflected priorities; Chairman & CEO Ball said, “our share price remains at a very attractive level,” and reiterated the intent to “reduce our leverage,” while adding the company continued to evaluate acquisitions “both in the UIP space as well as in the Performance Chemicals space.”

  • Garvit Bhandari, Singular Research: Asked about PC margin trajectory as copper hedges roll off; Chairman & CEO Ball said Q2 had “peak margins of roughly 22%,” Q3 was “roughly 18%,” and management expected “that to deteriorate a little bit further in the fourth quarter” ahead of 2027 pricing.

  • Garvit Bhandari, Singular Research: Asked whether the plan for PC plus RUPS to exceed 85% of sales by 2028 was organic or inorganic; Chairman & CEO Ball said, “we expect that to be primarily organic right now,” while adding, “if we are going to do anything on the inorganic side, it’s going to be in PC or UIP.”

Sentiment analysis

  • Analyst tone was slightly negative to neutral, with questions concentrating on pricing recovery timing, margin durability (notably in PC and RUPS), and capital allocation trade-offs; several were probing but not adversarial (e.g., requests to “work through each of the segments” on price increases and whether capex levels were “the new normal”).

  • Management tone was slightly positive but defensive on near-term profitability, repeatedly emphasizing cost pressure and timing lags while expressing confidence in 2027 recovery; Chairman & CEO Ball said “we are not minimizing” margin pressure (via CFO Brenner) and added, “we’re extremely confident on the PC piece,” while describing CM&C as “a little bit uncertain.”

  • Versus the prior quarter, management’s language shifted from executing transformation amid volatility to explicitly acknowledging an earnings reset: in Q2, management said, “Our broader outlook for the business remains intact,” while in Q3 it said rising costs “led us to revise our earnings outlook for the remainder of 2026.”

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Guidance moved lower in Q3: Q2 guided 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $240 million to $250 million and adjusted EPS of $3.80 to $4.20, while Q3 guided adjusted EBITDA of $220 million to $225 million and adjusted EPS of $3.10 to $3.25, with Q3 attributing the change to “higher input costs…continue throughout Q4.”

  • The Stickney plan advanced from an accelerated end-of-distillation target in Q2 to completed shutdown milestones in Q3, with Chairman & CEO Ball stating, “we recently reached 2 important milestones by ending distillation activities on September 30 and then discontinuing the remaining chemical production at Stickney in October.”

  • Analyst focus evolved from Catalyst pacing and general cost pass-through questions in Q2 to detailed 2027 pricing mechanics by segment in Q3, alongside more granular debate about margin pressure tied to Class I rail concessions and PC raw material inflation.

Risks and concerns

  • Management highlighted ongoing inflation and lags in recovery, with Chairman & CEO Leroy Ball stating the company was “absorbing higher raw material, additive, and logistics costs today before we are able to fully recover them through pricing.”

  • CM&C volatility remained a key risk, with CFO & Treasurer Eric Brenner citing “conflict in the Middle East and safety-related coal mine closures in China,” plus operational disruption from “the receipt of poor-quality tar” and “transition and logistics costs” during the network shift.

  • Rail profitability risk was tied to pricing concessions and demand variability, with management acknowledging “price concessions that we made to secure future volumes have pressured margins in the near term,” while positioning cost actions including workforce reductions and the Florence wind-down.

Final takeaway

Management described Q3 as a mix of volume resilience and market-share gains in Performance Chemicals and utility poles, but with profitability hit by faster-moving coal tar, copper, freight, and other input costs that could not be fully recovered in 2026 timing. The company lowered 2026 adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EPS guidance, while reiterating that pricing resets taking effect in January 2027 and structural actions—most visibly the completed Stickney shutdown milestones and ongoing network optimization—are expected to support improved earnings and continued cash generation into 2027.

data.title: Trending stocks this week as Wall Street ends sharply lower
data.description:
The U.S. stock market was marked this week by a historical midterm election result as Democrats took control of House and Senate.

In the immediate aftermath of the midterms, concerns about elevated AI valuations and heavy technology-sector spending triggered a sharp sell-off, particularly in semiconductor stocks.

Technology stocks rebounded on the last day of trade, but not enough to erase the week's losses. The major indices still ended the week in red. The S&P 500 was down around 3%, Nasdaq Composite declined 4% and Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.7%.

In economy-related news, the October U.S. jobs report showed stronger-than-expected job growth, raising expectations of a Fed rate hike in December, adding another source of uncertainty for equities.

Amid a turbulent week for Wall Street, here were some of the stocks that caught the attention of investors:

Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) dropped soon after the elections as Elon Musk's $500M bet on Republican campaigns proved unsuccessful. Both stocks rebounded somewhat on Friday but still ended in the red. Tesla was down 11.3% and SpaceX declined 2%. Musk also said on Friday that Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production in 2027 because of underwhelming sales.

AI and semiconductor stocks tumbled on Thursday as investors pulled back from technology stocks amid concerns over the outlook for data center spending following the U.S. midterm elections. The selloff came a day after Democrats secured a majority in Congress. Chipmakers bore the brunt of the declines. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell 17%, Intel (INTC) lost 10.3%, Broadcom (AVGO) declined 10.4%, Nvidia (NVDA) dropped 9.2%, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) fell 10.7%.

Marvell (MRVL) announced a definitive agreement to acquire Lumentum (LITE), an optical components manufacturer, in an all-stock transaction with an implied enterprise value of $115B. Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell common stock for each Lumentum share they own. The acquisition is intended to strengthen Marvell's position in AI data center connectivity and optical technologies.

AppLovin (APP) shares surged more than 31% following its third-quarter earnings announcement. Revenue increased 55% year over year to $2.185B, while net income climbed 72% to $1.44B. The strong results were driven in part by improvements to its AI-powered advertising technology.

Qualcomm's (QCOM) shares fell nearly 10% on Thursday after its smartphone chip revenue tumbled 26% in the fourth quarter as rising memory prices weighed on handset demand. Overall, Qualcomm said it earned an adjusted $2.17 per share in the quarter as revenue fell 7% year-over-year to come in at $10.44B.

Apple (AAPL) reported fiscal fourth-quarter results that topped Wall Street's estimates. For the period ending Sept. 26, Apple said it earned $2.10 per share as revenue rose 12% year-over-year to come in at $114.48B. However, shares slipped as Apple forecast gross margins of 45%–46% for the December quarter, down from 47.9% in the September quarter. Following the report, CEO John Ternus warned that memory-chip prices were rising at an unprecedented rate.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) shares fell even as the company reported strong third-quarter results and issued an upward revision to its full-year outlook, as investors focused on a slowdown in U.S. commercial bookings. U.S. commercial revenue surged 148% Y/Y to $984M in Q3, while U.S. government revenue jumped 96% to $953M.

Oracle (ORCL) priced a combined $20B stock and bond offering, including a $10B common stock sale at an 11.2% discount to its last closing price, as the company raises fresh capital amid its expanding AI infrastructure investments. The company priced 86.2M shares at $116 a piece, compared with its October 30 closing price of $130.67. The equity offering is expected to generate ~$9.9B in net proceeds. Separately, Oracle (ORCL) priced $10B of senior notes across five tranches.

AMD (AMD) reported third-quarter results and guidance that topped Wall Street's forecast. For the period ending Sept. 26, AMD said it earned an adjusted $2.09 per share as revenue rose 45% year-over-year to come in at $13.38B. Data Center revenue rose 97% year-over-year to $8.55B, aided by its MI-series AI accelerators and its Instinct and EPYC processors.

Novo (NVO) raised its outlook for the year once again, driven by continued demand for its Wegovy weight-loss pill, and its older shot Ozempic. The Danish drugmaker now expects sales and operating profit to either decline by 2% or increase by as much as 2% this year at constant exchange rates. The revised forecast compares with its previous outlook, which had projected declines of up to 6%.

data.title: Berkshire ramps up buybacks in Q3 even as operating earnings dip
data.description:
Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A) (BRK.B) has accelerated its stock buybacks during its third quarter ending Sept. 30, while the investing giant’s operating earnings fell amid weakness in its insurance businesses.

The Omaha, Nebraska-based conglomerate repurchased $9.6B in shares in Q3, ahead of Visible Alpha estimates of $1.6B, increasing its full-year stock buybacks to $14.4B.

Its Q3 buybacks have more than doubled from its Q2 2026 buybacks of $4.5B, which was also a sharp increase from its Q1 buybacks of $234M as the new CEO, Greg Abel, assumed leadership from billionaire investor Warren Buffett in January.

However, the company’s operating earnings for the period fell ~6% YoY to $12.7B, as operating earnings attributed to its insurance-underwriting business dropped ~43% YoY to $1.4B, driven by lower underwriting earnings at GEICO.

The vehicle and property insurance company added $982M in pre-tax underwriting earnings, down ~45% YoY, as its underwriting expenses rose ~17% YoY to $1.7B while losses and LAE jumped ~9% YoY to $8.7B.

The company's insurance-investment income, meanwhile, dropped ~14% YoY to $2.7B as interest and other investment income fell ~14% YoY mainly due to lower interest income, indicating lower short-term interest rates.

However, Berkshire's (BRK.A) railroad business, BNSF, added $1.7B with ~19% YoY growth, benefiting from higher shipping volumes and improved operating efficiencies, partially offset by higher fuel costs.

The company’s Energy business, meanwhile, generated $1.6B with an ~8% YoY growth thanks to higher earnings from the U.S. utilities and natural gas pipelines businesses. Its manufacturing, service, and retailing operations generated $4.0B with ~12% YoY growth driven by individual products and service businesses.

The company recorded $105.6B in revenue for the quarter, beating Visible Alpha estimates of $102B, with ~11% YoY growth as its insurance and other revenue climbed ~11% YoY to $91.0B.

data.title: The long, strange trip of Tesla's Cybertruck
data.description:
Elon Musk unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019 with a stainless-steel, angular design that looked unlike any pickup on the road. The event at Tesla's (TSLA) design studio in Hawthorne, California invoked a Blade Runner theme.

Originally, Tesla (TSLA) promised a starting price under $40K, a 500-mile top range, and production by 2021. Delays, redesigns, and manufacturing problems pushed deliveries back until late November 2023, and prices came in far higher than promised. Reddit (RDDT) co-founder Alexis Ohanian was among the first owners.

An early public demo of the Cybertruck is remembered for the “armor glass” windows that shattered when a steel ball was thrown at them. The early Foundation Series cost around $100K, and Tesla (TSLA) later added a cheaper all-wheel-drive trim and a rear-wheel-drive version in 2025.

In reality, demand never matched the hype. While Tesla (TSLA) claimed more than a million reservations, those were refundable deposits, and actual sales were only a fraction of that ambitious tally. During an earnings conference call, Musk once stated Tesla (TSLA) could build 250K trucks a year, yet annual sales reportedly stayed far below that. Kelley Blue Book estimated Cybertruck sales of 39K in 2024 and just over 20K in 2025. The electric truck's reputation was also dented by repeated recalls, including problems with the accelerator pedal and body panels. Finally, analysts noted Elon Musk's high-profile political activity may have curbed some demand.

The Cybertruck entered a field of electric and conventional pickups. Its closest rivals were the Rivian (RIVN) R1T and the Ford (F) F-150 Lightning. Chevrolet's (GM) Silverado EV and GMC's Hummer EV competed on range and luxury, and the Ram 1500 REV was another planned electric entrant. Of course, the Cybertruck also had to contend with the gas-powered F-150, Silverado, and Ram 1500, which have long dominated the truck market and offer more traditional towing and work capability.

Earlier in the week, Elon Musk said Tesla (TSLAA) will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production, which is Tesla's (TSLA) disruptive robotaxi.  The future of the Cybertruck plans remains unclear, although Elon Musk confirmed it was the end of an era in a X reply.  If the timeline holds, production would end roughly three and a half years after the first customer deliveries.

data.title: Anthropic IPO to move forward despite tech selloff: FT
data.description:
Anthropic (ANT) is pressing ahead with its plans for a U.S. public listing this month and is even prepared to accept a lower-than-expected valuation amid investor worries over an ongoing tech selloff, The Financial Times reported, citing multiple investors in the AI startup.

The Claude maker is racing towards its much-anticipated initial public offering before the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday this month, the investors said, adding that the company is planning to raise $80B-$100B at a valuation of $1.25T-$1.75T.

While that is a significant increase from its current $965B valuation, the target falls short of the doubled price tag investors had hoped for as recently as a month ago.

“My view is they will price it very conservatively, call it $1.5tn, and go up from there,” said one large investor. Others taking part in the deal expected even a lower valuation of roughly $1.3T.

Anthropic’s (ANT) scaled-back expectations coincide with a sharp decline in AI-related tech stocks over the recent weeks, a selloff that accelerated on Thursday when the Nasdaq 100 (QQQM) plunged 6.4% on worries over a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure buildout.

Bloomberg reported on Friday that OpenAI (OPENAI), which recently delayed its IPO plans, completed a new private funding round of roughly $11B, valuing the ChatGPT maker at $1.25T, a sharp decline from $30B or more it initially sought at a $1.4T valuation.

However, according to more than half a dozen Anthropic (ANT) investors, the company remains on track to go public even if its CEO Dario Amodei has to accept a price cut to achieve the goal.

“It’s just one milestone along the way,” one early investor of the company said. “They should treat it like every other fundraise: a means to an end.”

Multiple people familiar with Amodei’s thinking said that the CEO has shown little interest in beating Elon Musk’s SpaceX (SPCX), which completed the largest ever IPO in June at a valuation of roughly $1.8T. “They don’t care about being bigger than SpaceX or maximizing the IPO,” one investor noted.

“They’re donating the majority of their economics to charity anyway,” he added, referring to Anthropic co-founders’ intention to hand 80% of their personal equity in the company to charitable purposes.

With $150B in cash and liquid investments on its balance sheet, Anthropic (ANT) expects to raise enough funding so as not to sell equity again, people familiar with its thinking said.

“Public markets are highly averse to dilution,” added another large investor. “When you are taking a company public, that should be the last time you tap equity capital markets. But it opens the window for debt.”

JPMorgan (JPM), which leads U.S. retail sales of company shares, is expected to hold an “information session” for prospective investors on November 13, the FT said. Anthropic (ANT) declined to comment on the report.

data.title: The humanoid robot race heats up after Agility Robotics begins to trade
data.description:
Humanoid robot startup Agility Robotics (AGLT) began trading during the week. Shares were volatile in the first two days of action, showing an initial gain of more than 20% before settling back to closer to the $10 per share price used in the merger. Agility Robotics has the distinction of being the first U.S.-listed company focused purely on humanoid robots. It went public by merging with Churchill Capital Corp XI rather than through a traditional IPO.

The merger valued Agility’s existing equity at about $2.5B. The company brought in roughly $465M in gross capital before expenses. About $201M of that money comes from a private investment led by Foxconn (FXCOF). Nvidia (NVDA) and SoftBank Vision Fund 2 are also backers.

Agility (AGLT) highlighted that it expects to use the fresh funding to bring Digit 5 to market and expand manufacturing. Digit 5 is built to work safely near people without the safety barriers earlier versions needed. Deliveries are targeted for the first half of 2027, with general availability by the end of 2027. Digit is already deployed at nine customer facilities, including sites run by Amazon (AMZN), Toyota (TM), and GXO (GXO). The company plans to ramp up production at its RoboFab factory in Oregon and is building a new facility in Pittsburgh for software and AI work.

Agility Robotics (AGLT) expects annual losses to continue but has an order on its books worth more than $300M from one unnamed customer, covering 1K robots over three years. The contract requires Agility Robotics (AGLT) to hit delivery milestones and meet product specifications. Each Digit 5 robot will initially cost Agility about $150K in parts. The company expects that to drop to $75K at 1K robots a year and $30K at 10K a year.

Seeking Alpha analyst IPO Kitchen highlighted that Agility Robotics (AGLT) faces stiff competition from a number of competitors globally. In North America, the company's Digit 5 model will compete with Tesla's (TSLA) Optimus robot, Figure AI's 02 and 03 models, Boston Dynamics' Atlas robot, Apptronik's Apollo robot, 1X Technologies' NEO and EVE models, and Sanctuary AI's Phoenix robot. The list of competitors in Europe was noted to include Agile Robots, NEURA Robotics, and PAL Robotics, while in China, competition includes Unitree Robotics' H1 and G1 models, UBTECH Robotics' Walker robot, the Yuanzheng models from AgiBot/Zhiyuan Robotics, Fourier Intelligence's GR robot, and XPeng's (XPEV) IRON robot.

Telus targets $900M annualized cash savings exiting 2028 while projecting $500M AI infrastructure revenue over 3 years

Earnings Call Insights: TELUS (T:CA) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "Our transformation strategy has one clear objective, and that is to solidify TELUS' position as the leading communications and AI infrastructure player in Canada" (CEO, President & Director Victor Dodig). Dodig described "an intentional and a strategic pivot to profitable growth" built around strengthening the balance sheet, tightening operating discipline, and reallocating resources toward the core telecom business and AI infrastructure.
  • "We're committed to strengthening our balance sheet and have a clear path to achieving a net debt to adjusted EBITDA leverage ratio of 3x or lower by the end of 2028" (CEO, President & Director Dodig). He reiterated actions previously announced in Q2: "We reset our dividend payout ratio... terminated the dilutive discount on the dividend investment -- reinvestment plan, and we put a moratorium on acquisitions," while emphasizing a focus on "monetization strategy for our noncore assets" and "unlock equity value from our PureFibre network while maintaining control."
  • "Today, we are announcing a program that targets $900 million in annualized cash savings exiting 2028" (CEO, President & Director Dodig). He added that "Up to 80% of these run rate savings are expected to come from telecom," and cited additional consumer pivots, including moving "home security" and "TV offerings to a capital-light model" and "winding down unprofitable and capital-intensive initiatives," with "approximately $250 million in structural cash savings" expected to fully run-rate "beginning in 2027."
  • "Basic EPS was negative $0.42 due to the TELUS Health noncash impairment" (Chief Financial Officer Gopi Chande). Chande also reported "Consolidated service revenue of $4.5 billion" and "Consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $1.8 billion," plus "free cash flow of $396 million" and leverage of "3.6x" as of September 30.

Outlook

  • "For the full year 2026, we are reaffirming our consolidated guidance as updated with our Q2 results in July" (CFO Chande). He restated: "service revenue of flat to negative 2%, adjusted EBITDA of negative 2% to negative 4%, capital expenditures of approximately $2.6 billion and free cash flow of approximately $1.8 billion."
  • "We have a pipeline today of more than $1 billion in total contract value across our digital infrastructure business" (CEO, President & Director Dodig). Dodig added, "over the next 3 years, we project about $500 million in revenue with healthy margins," and management clarified in Q&A that "$500 million" is "a cumulative number" (EVP and President of Business Solutions, Health, Agriculture, Consumer Goods & Partner Solutions Navin Arora).
  • Compared with Q2, management did not introduce a new full-year 2026 range, maintaining the July update; the Q3 call added a detailed multi-year efficiency target and more explicit AI infrastructure revenue framing.

Financial Results

  • "Consolidated service revenue of $4.5 billion was lower by 1% year-over-year" (CFO Chande), while "Consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $1.8 billion declined by 5%," which he said was "primarily due to weaker results in TELUS Digital" and the prior-year impact of "$78 million of onetime items."
  • "Mobile phone net additions of 84,000" and "blended mobile phone churn landing at 1.01% for the quarter" were highlighted as key operating metrics, alongside "postpaid churn" that "improved to below 0.9%" (CFO Chande). He also said "Mobile network revenue of $1.8 billion was up 1%" and "Fixed data revenue of $1.2 billion increased by 2%."
  • "We recorded a noncash goodwill impairment of $800 million for our TELUS Health business" (CFO Chande). He attributed it to "updated growth expectations, broader market conditions and current valuation perspectives from ongoing strategic processes," while stating, "it does not change our commitment to TELUS Health."
  • "In order to achieve the $900 million target, we expect to invest approximately $150 million" (CFO Chande), and he reported liquidity of "$3 billion" and a quarterly dividend of "$0.1875 per share."

Q&A

  • Maher Yaghi, Scotiabank: asked about "the revenue opportunity for TELUS" and "where... growth could come from"; CEO Dodig said the plan combines "$900 million" cash savings, "monetize our noncore assets," and "unlock some of the equity value" in PureFibre, while EVP David Fuller added, "we can continue to grow the telecom business in the low single digits... both top and bottom line going forward."
  • Drew McReynolds, RBC: probed the composition of "$900 million"; CFO Chande said the split is "roughly 50-50 CapEx and EBITDA," defined as "$75 million in December 2028 times 12," with "$150 million" of upfront investment; Drew also asked about the "$500 million" AI revenue number, and Arora replied, "That is a cumulative number."
  • Stephanie Price, CIBC: asked about PureFibre equitization and "retaining control"; CFO Chande said the aim is to "surface the significant value" to "strengthen our balance sheet," while Fuller stated, "we are going to absolutely maintain control" and "it is not... focused on the wholesale side of the business."
  • Vince Valentini, TD Cowen: pressed on wireless quality and Public Mobile; Fuller responded, "Q3 was actually a very restrained approach to promotional intensity," adding, "our success on net adds was entirely driven by our success in churn" and "it was not driven by Public loading at all."
  • Tim Casey, BMO: asked to reconcile a prior "$2 billion" AI narrative versus current "$500 million"; CEO Dodig said the company made "a refinement to our strategic narrative," and Arora said the earlier framing "included a lot of the TELUS digital elements" that have been removed from the current infrastructure-focused pillars.
  • David McFadgen, ATB Cormark: asked what TELUS Health is "worth now" post-impairment and about eliminating the DRIP; CFO Chande said, "I'm not going to comment on the specific valuation of TELUS Health," and on the DRIP, "it's not something that's on our radar right now" due to "low uptake."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Slightly negative analyst tone centered on proof of savings, valuation, and AI sizing, including questions like "How do we square that" and requests for valuation "ballpark" (Tim Casey, BMO; David McFadgen, ATB Cormark).
  • Slightly positive management tone emphasized execution confidence, including "We know how to do this, and we're going to get it done" (CEO, President & Director Dodig) and "we're confident in its delivery" (CFO Chande), while avoiding valuation specifics ("stay away from anchoring on any valuation," CFO Chande).
  • Versus Q2, Q3 carried a more concrete, quantified operational-efficiency posture (explicit $900M target) and more pointed analyst scrutiny on reconciling AI opportunity sizing and impairment implications.

Quarter-over-quarter Comparison

  • Q3 introduced a new quantified efficiency program: "targets $900 million in annualized cash savings exiting 2028" (CEO, President & Director Dodig), whereas in Q2 Dodig said, "I expect to provide a detailed overview... on or before our third quarter earnings call in November" (CEO, President & Director Dodig).
  • Q3 added a specific AI infrastructure revenue framing: "we project about $500 million in revenue" over 3 years (CEO, President & Director Dodig), while Q2 focused on building "sustainable sovereign AI data centers" without giving a comparable multi-year revenue projection in prepared remarks (CEO, President & Director Dodig).
  • Impairments shifted from TELUS Digital in Q2 ("pretax noncash carrying value impairment of $2.1 billion," CFO Chande) to TELUS Health in Q3 ("noncash goodwill impairment of $800 million," CFO Chande), with both calls tying impairments to changing expectations and market conditions.

Risks and Concerns

  • "Service revenue... was lower by 1%" and EBITDA pressure were linked to "weaker results in TELUS Digital" and "hyperscale client volume ramp-downs" (CFO Chande), with management framing mitigation as tighter pricing/terms, automation, and overhead reduction (CEO, President & Director Dodig).
  • Management cited execution and timing risk around monetization and fiber equitization, stressing control and process discipline: "We'll manage these engagements on our terms" (CEO, President & Director Dodig) and "we're still defining our perimeter" (CFO Chande).
  • On AI infrastructure, management emphasized disciplined pacing: "use the assets we have first, then add GPU capacity as customer demand materializes" (CEO, President & Director Dodig) and "we're not going to boil the ocean" (EVP Arora).

Final Takeaway

TELUS management framed Q3 as a shift from outlining a transformation to quantifying it, anchored by a $900 million annualized cash-savings program exiting 2028, continued deleveraging toward 3x net debt to adjusted EBITDA by 2028, and a Canadian-focused AI infrastructure plan that includes a pipeline of more than $1 billion in total contract value and a projected $500 million of cumulative revenue over the next 3 years. Management paired these targets with reaffirmed 2026 guidance ranges from Q2, while acknowledging pressure in TELUS Digital and recording an $800 million noncash TELUS Health goodwill impairment tied to updated expectations and market conditions.
